meta.titre: Classification of Organisms: Taxonomy, Phylogeny and the Animal Phyla

sections.contenu_markdown: The Limbe Botanic Garden and the forests of Korup hold thousands of species, and a scientist who finds a new insect there must be able to say exactly what it is and where it belongs. Biologists everywhere use the same system, so a researcher in Yaoundé and one in Leeds mean the same animal when they write its name. The GCE Advanced Level paper tests your knowledge of the hierarchy, of how names are written, of the types of classification and of the features that define the main phyla. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and a method for identifying a specimen.

items: Living organisms are made of cells, which may be prokaryotic or eukaryotic.
Fossils and DNA provide evidence of evolution from common ancestors.
Heterotrophs feed on organic matter made by other organisms, while autotrophs make their own.
A segmented body is made of repeated sections.

sections.titre: The taxonomic hierarchy, naming, types of classification and the main animal phyla
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Taxonomy** is the science of naming and classifying organisms. A group at any level is a **taxon**. The hierarchy runs from the largest to the smallest group: **Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species**. Each taxon contains one or more taxa of the rank below it.

A **species** is a group of organisms with similar features that can interbreed to produce **fertile offspring**. The **binomial system** gives each species a two-part Latin name: the **genus** with a capital initial and the **species** with a small initial, both italic or underlined, for example *Homo sapiens*.

**Types of classification.** An **artificial** system uses a few easily seen features (such as 'lives in water'). A **natural** system uses many shared features. A **phylogenetic** system groups organisms according to their **evolutionary relationships**, using fossils and molecular evidence such as DNA base sequences and amino acid sequences of proteins; the more similar the molecules, the more recently the species shared an ancestor.

**Kingdoms.** Prokaryotae (bacteria), Protoctista, Fungi (chitin cell walls, absorb food), Plantae and Animalia. In the three-domain system the prokaryotes are split into Bacteria and Archaea, with Eukarya for all other organisms.

**Animal phyla and key features**

| Phylum | Key features |
|---|---|
| Porifera (sponges) | pores, no true tissues, no symmetry |
| Cnidaria | radial symmetry, **two cell layers** (diploblastic), stinging cells, one opening |
| Platyhelminthes | flat body, three layers (triploblastic), no body cavity, one opening to the gut |
| Nematoda | cylindrical, unsegmented, tapering ends, tough cuticle, three layers, mouth and anus |
| Annelida | segmented, bristles (chaetae), true coelom, three layers |
| Arthropoda | jointed appendages, chitin exoskeleton (cuticle), segmented, three layers |
| Mollusca | soft body, muscular foot, mantle, often a shell |
| Echinodermata | marine, spiny skin, five-part radial symmetry in the adult, tube feet |
| Chordata | notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits at some stage |

variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions asking you to assign an arthropod to a class.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
- **Insecta**: three body regions (head, thorax, abdomen), **three pairs of legs**, one pair of antennae, usually wings.
- **Arachnida**: two body regions (cephalothorax and abdomen), **four pairs of legs**, no antennae (spiders, scorpions, ticks).
- **Crustacea**: two pairs of antennae, five or more pairs of legs, mostly aquatic (crabs, prawns).
- **Myriapoda**: long body with many segments, one or two pairs of legs per segment (centipedes, millipedes).

variantes.nom: Using and building a dichotomous key
variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions where you must identify a specimen or write a key.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A **dichotomous key** is a series of numbered pairs of contrasting statements (couplets). Each statement describes a feature that can be seen and either leads to another couplet or to a name. Rules: use features that are easy to observe, avoid size or colour that varies, use opposites ('present' and 'absent'), and always give two choices.

sections.enonce_markdown: A student collects an animal in a garden. It has a body in two regions, a cephalothorax and an abdomen, and eight jointed legs. It has no antennae and no wings. Its body is covered by a hard exoskeleton that contains chitin, and its body is bilaterally symmetrical. (a) State the phylum and give two features that support the choice. (b) Place it in a class by counting the pairs of legs. (c) The genus is Araneus and the species is diadematus. Write the scientific name correctly. (d) Write the full classification from kingdom downwards if the order is Araneae and the family is Araneidae.

etapes.justification: The animal is multicellular and feeds on other animals, so it belongs to the animal kingdom; the symmetry removes sponges and cnidarians.
Jointed legs, a segmented body and a chitin exoskeleton are the features of arthropods.
Count the legs: eight legs make four pairs; the body has two regions and there are no antennae.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Eight legs = four pairs, so the class is **Arachnida** (not Insecta, which has three pairs).

etapes.justification: The genus has a capital letter and the species a small letter; both are in italics or underlined.
List the ranks from largest to smallest.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Kingdom Animalia; Phylum Arthropoda; Class Arachnida; Order Araneae; Family Araneidae; Genus *Araneus*; species *diadematus*.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Features such as jointed legs and a chitin exoskeleton give the phylum Arthropoda; four pairs of legs and two body regions give the class Arachnida, and the binomial name is Araneus diadematus.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing the name of a species as 'homo Sapiens' or 'Homo Sapiens'.
items.pourquoi_faux: In the binomial system only the genus starts with a capital letter; the species name is all in lower case.
items.correction_markdown: Write *Homo sapiens* (italics) or Homo sapiens underlined.

items.erreur_markdown: A horse and a donkey belong to the same species because they can mate.
items.pourquoi_faux: A species is defined by producing fertile offspring. A mule is the offspring of a horse and a donkey and is sterile.
items.correction_markdown: The horse and the donkey are different species; interbreeding is not enough, the offspring must be **fertile**.

items.erreur_markdown: All worms belong to one phylum.
items.pourquoi_faux: Flatworms, roundworms and segmented worms differ in body shape, segmentation and body cavity, and are placed in Platyhelminthes, Nematoda and Annelida.
items.correction_markdown: Use the features: flat and unsegmented, cylindrical with a cuticle, or divided into segments.

items.erreur_markdown: Fungi are plants because they do not move.
items.pourquoi_faux: Fungi have chitin cell walls and feed heterotrophically by absorbing digested food, whereas plants contain chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis.

items.erreur_markdown: Phylogenetic classification groups organisms that look alike.
items.pourquoi_faux: Phylogenetic classification groups organisms according to their evolutionary relationships. Similar appearance may arise by convergent evolution.
items.correction_markdown: Phylogeny is based on **common ancestry**, supported by fossils and molecular data.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Arrange these taxa from the largest to the smallest: class, genus, kingdom, order, phylum, species, family. (b) Which of these scientific names is correctly written: Panthera Leo, panthera leo, Panthera leo? (c) What is the meaning of a 'diploblastic' animal and which phylum is an example?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species**.

(b) **Panthera leo** (capital for the genus, small letter for the species, in italics or underlined).

(c) A diploblastic animal has a body wall made of **two cell layers** (ectoderm and endoderm); an example is the phylum **Cnidaria**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Use the key to identify specimens P, Q and R.

1a Body has jointed legs: go to 4. 1b Body has no jointed legs: go to 2.
2a Body divided into ring-like segments: **earthworm**. 2b Body not segmented: go to 3.
3a Body flat and ribbon-like: **flatworm**. 3b Body cylindrical, tapered at both ends, with a tough cuticle: **roundworm**.
4a Four pairs of legs and no antennae: **spider**. 4b Not four pairs of legs: go to 5.
5a Three pairs of legs and one pair of antennae: **insect**. 5b Five or more pairs of legs and two pairs of antennae: **crustacean**.

P: ring-like segments, no legs, bristles on the body. Q: ten jointed legs, two pairs of antennae, lives in a stream. R: six jointed legs, one pair of antennae, two pairs of wings. (a) Identify P, Q and R, stating the numbers of the couplets used. (b) Give the phylum of each. (c) Give one reason why a feature such as 'small' would be a poor choice in a key.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **P**: 1b, then 2a: **earthworm**. **Q**: 1a, 4b (ten legs is not four pairs), then 5b (five pairs of legs and two pairs of antennae): **crustacean**. **R**: 1a, 4b, 5a (three pairs of legs, one pair of antennae): **insect**.

(b) P: **Annelida**. Q and R: **Arthropoda**.

(c) 'Small' is relative, depends on age, and cannot be measured by the user, so two people could answer differently.

items.enonce_markdown:
A protein of 100 amino acids is sequenced in five species A to E. The table gives the number of amino acid differences between each pair (illustrative data).

| | B | C | D | E |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 4 | 12 | 12 | 27 |
| B | | 14 | 14 | 28 |
| C | | | 3 | 27 |
| D | | | | 27 |

(a) Which two species are most closely related? (b) Calculate the mean number of differences between the group A, B and the group C, D. (c) Draw conclusions about the pattern of branching (describe a cladogram in words). (d) Explain why such molecular data are used in phylogenetic classification.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) C and D, with only **3 differences** (3 %), the smallest number in the table.

(b) Differences between the groups: 12, 12, 14 and 14. Mean = (12 + 12 + 14 + 14) / 4 = 52 / 4 = **13 differences**.

(c) A and B are a pair (4 differences) and C and D are a pair (3 differences). The two pairs are 13 differences apart on average, so they share a more recent common ancestor with each other than with E, which differs from all four by 27 or 28, so **E branched off first**. The cladogram is ((A, B), (C, D)), E.

(d) Differences accumulate by mutation over time, so the fewer the differences the more recently two species shared a common ancestor. Molecular data are objective, can be compared for organisms that look very different, and are not affected by convergent evolution.

items_markdown: Hierarchy: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
A species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring; its binomial name has a capital genus and a small species, in italics or underlined.
Phylogenetic classification is based on evolutionary relationships, using fossils and molecular data such as DNA and protein sequences.
Diploblastic animals have two cell layers (Cnidaria); triploblastic animals have three. Nematoda and Arthropoda have a cuticle.
Arthropod classes are found by counting body regions, legs and antennae.
A dichotomous key uses paired, observable, contrasting features.
